# The Space Between Thoughts

I'm sitting in that peculiar moment where the day hasn't quite decided what it wants to be. The coffee is still warm but no longer steaming, which feels like a metaphor for something, though I can't quite grasp what. Maybe that's the point. Maybe some things aren't meant to be grasped, only observed as they cool.

There's a bird outside that keeps returning to the same branch. I've watched it land, take off, circle back three times now. Either it forgot something or it's the most indecisive bird in existence. I relate to this bird more than I'd like to admit. How many times have I returned to the same decision, hoping a different answer might be waiting there?

I've been thinking about the word "nostalgia" lately. We use it to describe this ache for the past, but I wonder if what we're really nostalgic for is the person we were when those memories were being made. We can't go back to the moments, obviously, but more than that—we can't go back to the versions of ourselves who inhabited them. I'm grieving someone I used to be just as much as I'm grieving a time that's passed. That seems important somehow.

Writing is strange. You sit with a blank space—whether it's a page or a screen—and you negotiate with it. You make an offer: "Here's what I'm thinking. Will you help me shape it into something?" And sometimes the blank space says yes, and sometimes it just stares back. Today feels like a yes-day, even though I'm not entirely sure what I'm saying.

I read somewhere that octopuses have neurons throughout their arms, which means each arm is partly autonomous. They can make decisions without consulting their central brain. I find this comforting for reasons I can't fully articulate. It suggests that we don't need to have everything figured out in the thinking part of ourselves. Our bodies know things. Our hands know things. That split between intellect and instinct—maybe it's not a bug in our design; maybe it's a feature.

The world feels heavy lately. Not in the way that demands solutions, but in the way that asks you to sit with it for a while. We're all carrying things. Some of us are good at naming what we carry, and some of us just feel the weight and can't quite put it into words. Both are valid responses to living, I think. Both are ways of moving through.

I've been wondering about the stories we tell ourselves about who we are. How much of my personality is actually me, and how much is just a story I've been telling myself for so long that it feels like truth? If I decided tomorrow that I was a different kind of person, how long would it take before that became real? Can we become ourselves backwards, retroactively, by changing how we see ourselves going forward? These are probably the kinds of questions that don't have satisfying answers, which is exactly why I keep asking them.

There's something beautiful about impermanence that we don't talk about enough. We spend so much energy trying to hold onto things—moments, people, versions of ourselves—but everything is already leaving. Everything is already gone the moment it arrives. And somehow, knowing this makes the present moment feel less disposable, not more. If this is all we get, this breath, this cup of coffee, this bird circling its branch, then maybe it deserves more attention than I usually give it.

I think about all the small decisions that led me to this exact moment. The specific way I walked down the stairs this morning. The particular coffee beans I chose. The exact second I looked out the window. Infinite tiny divergence points that created this specific now. Sometimes this makes me feel small and insignificant, and sometimes it makes me feel like a miracle. Usually both at once.

Language is both the best and worst tool we have. It lets us reach across the space between people and say, "Here. This is what I'm feeling. Do you know this too?" But it also fails constantly. The thing I mean to express always seems slightly too big for the words available. It's like trying to pour the ocean into a cup. You might get some of it, but mostly you're just going to make a mess. And yet we keep trying, because what else do we have?

I'm interested in the concept of enough. How do we know when we have enough? Enough money, enough success, enough love, enough time. We set targets, but they keep moving. We achieve them, and suddenly they seem insufficient. There's always another level, another benchmark. But then there are these moments—unexpected, unearned—where you're just satisfied. Not thrilled. Not striving. Just satisfied. I wonder if I could practice that. If I could get better at recognizing it and sitting with it before the reaching starts again.

The bird is gone now. I wasn't watching when it left. It just disappeared into the greater world, pursuing whatever octopi pursue—I mean, whatever birds pursue. See? My brain is already tired. Words are sliding around inside my head like they're not attached to meaning anymore.

But that's okay. Not everything has to mean something. Sometimes things can just be. This writing. This moment. This sense of standing at the edge of understanding without quite falling into it. Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's the whole point—to sit in the space between thoughts and let ourselves just be here, in the not-knowing, in the not-having-it-figured-out, in the almost-but-not-quite.

The coffee's cold now. Time to move on.
